svg.title: Exchange surfaces
svg.desc: Why exchange systems?: Single cells: large SA:V; their outer surface can meet exchange needs. Large multicellular organisms: lower SA:V, long diffusion distances → specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. Surface area : volume: Cube side a: SA = 6a²; V = a³. 1 cm cube: 6 ÷ 1 = 6:1. 3 cm cube: 54 ÷ 27 = 2:1. Larger cube: more total area, less area per unit volume. Cutting into pieces exposes more area without changing total volume. Lung alveoli: Many tiny air sacs → large area; thin alveolar/capillary walls → short path. Blood supply and ventilation maintain steep gradients. O₂: air → blood. CO₂: blood → air. An alveolus is one air sac, not a lung. Small intestine: Villi/microvilli: large area. Thin lining: short diffusion distance. Blood removes absorbed substances, maintaining gradients. Sugars can enter blood by active transport against a gradient. Fish gills: Many filaments/lamellae → large area; thin surfaces → short diffusion distance. Blood carries substances to/from the surface; flowing water maintains gradients. O₂: water → blood; CO₂ moves out. Plant roots: Root hairs: large contact area with soil. Water enters by osmosis through a partially permeable membrane. Minerals can enter against the gradient by active transport, using respiration energy. Plant leaves: Broad → large area. Thin → short diffusion distance. Stomata let gases in/out; internal air spaces shorten paths. For photosynthesis: CO₂ enters, O₂ can diffuse out. State substance and direction in context. Explain the adaptation: Large area: more particles cross at once. Thin barrier: shorter diffusion path. Blood supply: brings/removes substances to maintain gradients. Ventilation: refreshes air/water. Link adaptation → effect → faster exchange.
